Strongyloidiasis is a human parasitic disease caused by the nematode called  Strongyloides stercoralis  , or sometimes the closely related  S. fülleborni . These helminths belong to a group of nematodes called roundworms. These intestinal worms can cause a number of symptoms in people, principally skin symptoms, abdominal pain , diarrhea and weight loss, but also many other specific and vague symptoms in disseminated disease, and severe life-threatening conditions through hyperinfection. In some people, particularly those who require corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive medication,  Strongyloides can cause a  hyperinfection syndrome that can lead to death if untreated. The diagnosis is made by blood and stool tests. The medication ivermectin is widely used to treat strongyloidiasis.

Pulmonary symptoms (including Löfflers syndrome) can occur during pulmonary migration of the filariform larvae. Pulmonary infiltrate may be present through radiological investigation. Dermatologic manifestations include urticarial rashes in the buttocks and waist areas as well as larva currens.

  Given the poor ability of stool examination to diagnose  Strongyloides , detecting antibodies by ELISA can be useful.  Serology can cross-react with other parasites, remain positive for years after successful treatment or be falsely negative in immunocompromised patients.    Infected patients will also often have an elevated eosinophil count, with an average of absolute eosinophil count of 1000 in one series.  Eosinophilia of a gastrointestinal infection may fluctuate in response to larval output, or may be permanently lacking in some disseminated infections. Hence lack of eosinophilia is not evidence of absence of infection. The combination of clinical suspicion, a positive antibody and a peripheral eosinophilia can be strongly suggestive of infection. ceramic.title: Larva Currens and Skin Symptoms of Strongyloides
ceramic.snippet:
Strongyloides stercoralis is the only intestinal parasite that produces a pathognomonic skin sign visible to the naked eye:  larva currens , a racing urticarial wheal that moves 5–10 cm per hour under the skin. This racing rash, along with perianal itch, chronic urticaria, Löffler's syndrome, and peripheral eosinophilia, makes up the cutaneous and allergic signature of  Strongyloides infection that can distinguish it from dozens of other causes of abdominal complaints. Recognizing these skin and immune signs is often the key to diagnosing an infection that otherwise has no unique laboratory fingerprint.

  Perianal itch from  Strongyloides is easily confused with other common causes of pruritus ani: hemorrhoids, fungal infection, pinworm ( Enterobius vermicularis ) infestation, contact dermatitis, and poor hygiene. A key distinguishing feature is that  Strongyloides -related perianal itch in someone from an endemic region will not respond to topical antifungals, hydrocortisone, or anti-pinworm therapy. Failure of these conventional treatments, combined with eosinophilia or a history of episodic racing rash, should prompt serological testing for  Strongyloides .

  Löffler's syndrome refers to a clinical syndrome of transient pulmonary infiltrates associated with peripheral eosinophilia, caused by larval migration through the lungs.

  An absolute eosinophil count above  500 cells/μL in a patient from an endemic region, or with a compatible history, warrants evaluation for helminthic infection.  Strongyloides should be high on the list because of its clinical importance in immunocompromised settings. Other helminths causing eosinophilia include  Toxocara ,  Ascaris , hookworm, and filarial species, but none of these carry the same acute risk of hyperinfection if the patient is immunosuppressed.

## Evaluation

Evaluation for S stercoralis infection should be guided by epidemiologic risk, clinical presentation, and host immune status. A high index of suspicion is required, particularly in individuals from endemic areas, those with unexplained eosinophilia, or patients who are immunosuppressed or about to receive immunosuppressive therapy. Screening is recommended before initiating corticosteroids, biologic agents, or other immunosuppressive therapies in at-risk individuals, as early detection and treatment can prevent hyperinfection syndrome and its associated high mortality.

The diagnosis of S stercoralis infection is challenging because larval excretion is often low and intermittent, resulting in low sensitivity of stool microscopy and low specificity of serology. No single gold-standard test or universally accepted diagnostic reference method exists. [27] In practice, stool examination, in combination with serologic testing and molecular methods, is recommended, particularly in patients with compatible epidemiologic exposure or unexplained eosinophilia. [27] Peripheral eosinophilia is common in chronic infection but lacks sensitivity and may be absent in severe disease. Notably, eosinophilia is often absent in hyperinfection syndrome. [28] [29]

linkup.snippet:
# When to Consider Ivermectin Treatment for Strongyloides stercoralis  
**Initiate ivermectin 200 μg/kg immediately in any patient with suspected or confirmed strongyloidiasis who is about to start or is currently on immunosuppressive therapy, particularly corticosteroids, as this prevents potentially fatal hyperinfection syndrome.** [1](#ref-1), [2](#ref-2)
### Asymptomatic Eosinophilia in Travelers/Migrants  
**Treat empirically with ivermectin 200 μg/kg plus albendazole 400 mg (single doses)** for:  
- Asymptomatic eosinophilia with negative stool microscopy in patients >24 months from endemic areas [2](#ref-2)
- Travelers returning from endemic regions with unexplained eosinophilia [2](#ref-2)  
**Important**: Stool microscopy has low sensitivity for Strongyloides (concentrated stool misses many cases). Serology or PCR are preferred diagnostics, but empirical treatment is reasonable while awaiting results [2](#ref-2), [7](#ref-7).
## Diagnostic Pitfalls  
**Normal or low eosinophil counts do NOT exclude strongyloidiasis**, especially in:  
- Hyperinfection syndrome (eosinophilia often absent) [11](#ref-11)
- Immunocompromised patients [11](#ref-11)
- Acute severe disease [2](#ref-2)  
**Stool microscopy limitations**: Intermittent larval output causes false negatives. Serology (sensitivity 92-98%) or PCR/mNGS of respiratory specimens (when available) provide faster, more reliable diagnosis [2](#ref-2), [11](#ref-11), [7](#ref-7).

Strongyloides stercoralis infections are frequently asymptomatic. Gastrointestinal symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, heartburn, nausea, loss of appetite and diarrhea. Dermatologic manifestations include urticarial rashes (recurrent raised red rash) in the buttocks and waist areas, where the Strongyloides worm entered the skin. Treatment for strongyloidiasis is recommended for all persons found to be infected, whether symptomatic or not, due to the risk of developing hyperinfection syndrome and/or disseminated strongyloidiasis. Furthermore, it is recommended that patients be considered for testing prior to being initiated on any immunosuppressive therapy, particularly corticosteroids.

A patient with vague abdominal symptoms, intermittent eosinophilia, and a history of residence in the tropics may look like a routine parasitology question. This article is for exam preparation and clinical revision. It is not a substitute for local guidelines, specialist infectious diseases advice, or patient-specific management.

Skin contact with contaminated soil is the classic route of acquisition.

## Overview of the organism and why it matters in the exam

*S. stercoralis* is an intestinal nematode with one feature that makes it stand apart from many other helminths: **autoinfection**. The parasite can complete part of its life cycle within the human host, allowing infection to persist for decades after exposure.

That single fact explains much of its clinical importance:

- Infection may present years after leaving an endemic region.

- Stool microscopy can be negative despite true infection.

- Eosinophilia may be absent in severe disseminated disease.

- Corticosteroids can trigger hyperinfection, even after short courses.

- Screening matters before transplantation, chemotherapy, biological therapy, and prolonged steroids.

The disease caused by the parasite is called **Strongyloidosis**. It ranges from asymptomatic carriage to life-threatening hyperinfection and dissemination.
